Seminar Title:

Ritual Performance and the Production of Urban Space: A Literary Urban Studies (LUS) Approach to Festival Placemaking in Odisha

Seminar Type:

Progress Seminar

Department:

Humanities and Social Sciences

Speaker Name:

Anisha Sahoo ( Rollno : 524hs1003)

Speaker Type:

Venue:

HS Seminar Room (MN436)

Date and Time:

Contact:

Seemita Mohanty

Abstract:

Urban spaces are continually shaped by social interactions, cultural practices, collective memory, and everyday experiences. Ritual festivals play a significant role in this process, transforming familiar streets, marketplaces, and public spaces into sites of performance, participation, and shared cultural meaning. Situated within the interdisciplinary framework of Literary Urban Studies (LUS), this research examines how ritual festivals in Odisha contribute to the production of urban space through narrative, performance, and recurring practices of placemaking. Drawing on Henri Lefebvre's theory of spatial production, alongside perspectives from performance studies and spatial humanities, the study explores how festivals reshape everyday urban environments and influence collective identity, memory, and belonging. It focuses on three cultural performances in Odisha: Dhanuyatra in Bargarh, Shital Shasthi in Sambalpur, and Budhi Thakurani Yatra in Berhampur. Through these cases, the research investigates how mythic narratives, ritual processions, symbolic authority, and community participation create distinctive forms of urban experience. The study also considers the changing rhythms of urban life before, during, and after festivals. In this context, emerging research on the post-festival ecology of Dhanuyatra (Sahoo &amp Mohanty, 2026)&nbsp highlights the intersections of ritual performance, waste generation, sanitation labour, environmental responsibility, and urban inequality. Such perspectives draw attention to the infrastructural arrangements and labour practices involved in restoring everyday civic environments following large-scale cultural celebrations. They further reveal how the responsibilities associated with post-festival recovery may be unevenly distributed across social groups, thereby complicating understandings of festivals as uniformly inclusive processes of placemaking and collective belonging.By examining preparation, performance, and post-festival recovery as interconnected processes, the research seeks to understand how festivals shape urban continuity while revealing differences in participation, access, and responsibility. It aims to contribute to Literary Urban Studies by foregrounding ritual performance and cyclical placemaking within Odisha's non-metropolitan urban contexts.
